claim: Glycolysis enzymes assemble into singular cytoplasmic granules called glycolytic (G) bodies in hypoxic stress conditions.
source: In hypoxic stress conditions, glycolysis enzymes assemble into singular cytoplasmic granules called glycolytic (G) bodies.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: G body formation in yeast correlates with increased glucose consumption and cell survival.
source: G body formation in yeast correlates with increased glucose consumption and cell survival.
evidence: This correlation is stated in the abstract as an observed relationship.

claim: Glycolysis enzymes are non-canonical RNA binding proteins.
source: We demonstrate that glycolysis enzymes are non-canonical RNA binding proteins, sharing many common mRNA substrates that are also integral constituents of G bodies.
evidence: The manuscript presents PAR-CL-MS and PAR-CLIP-seq data demonstrating RNA binding by glycolysis enzymes.

claim: Glycolysis enzymes share many common mRNA substrates.
source: We demonstrate that glycolysis enzymes are non-canonical RNA binding proteins, sharing many common mRNA substrates that are also integral constituents of G bodies.
evidence: PAR-CLIP-seq data shows overlap in mRNA substrates bound by different glycolysis enzymes.

claim: mRNA substrates of glycolysis enzymes are integral constituents of G bodies.
source: We demonstrate that glycolysis enzymes are non-canonical RNA binding proteins, sharing many common mRNA substrates that are also integral constituents of G bodies.
evidence: G body RIP-seq and smFISH data demonstrate mRNA localization to G bodies.

claim: RNA nucleates G body formation.
source: Targeting nonspecific endoribonucleases to G bodies reveals that RNA nucleates G body formation and maintains its structural integrity.
evidence: Experiments with targeted RNases show inhibition of G body formation.

claim: RNA maintains G body structural integrity.
source: Targeting nonspecific endoribonucleases to G bodies reveals that RNA nucleates G body formation and maintains its structural integrity.
evidence: Targeting RNases to pre-formed G bodies results in fragmentation into multiple puncta.

claim: Recruitment of glycolysis enzymes to G bodies relies on multivalent homotypic and heterotypic interactions.
source: Consistent with a phase separation mechanism of biogenesis, recruitment of glycolysis enzymes to G bodies relies on multivalent homotypic and heterotypic interactions.
evidence: Deletion studies of Pfk2 domains and analysis of Pfk1 recruitment demonstrate requirement for multiple interaction domains.

claim: G bodies fuse in vivo.
source: Furthermore, G bodies fuse in vivo and are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, consistent with a hydrogel-like composition.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging of mating cells shows G body fusion events.

claim: G bodies are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol.
source: Furthermore, G bodies fuse in vivo and are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, consistent with a hydrogel-like composition.
evidence: Treatment with 1,6-hexanediol does not fully dissolve G bodies, unlike P bodies.

claim: G bodies have a hydrogel-like composition.
source: Furthermore, G bodies fuse in vivo and are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, consistent with a hydrogel-like composition.
evidence: The insensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol and slow fusion dynamics are consistent with gel-like properties.

claim: RNA nucleates phase separation of the glycolysis machinery in response to hypoxic stress.
source: Taken together, our results elucidate the biophysical nature of G bodies and demonstrate that RNA nucleates phase separation of the glycolysis machinery in response to hypoxic stress.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including RNase targeting, multivalent interactions, and fusion dynamics support this conclusion.

claim: Liquid-like structures formed through phase separation display fast internal rearrangements, undergo fusion and fission, and exchange components with the surrounding solvent.
source: Liquid-like structures formed through phase separation of protein polymers display fast internal rearrangements, undergo fusion and fission, and exchange components with the surrounding solvent (Alberti et al., 2019; Hyman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Glycolysis enzymes coalesce into membraneless cytoplasmic granules called glycolytic bodies (G bodies) in hypoxic stress in yeast, C. elegans, and mammalian cells.
source: Recently, we and others demonstrated that glycolysis enzymes coalesce into membraneless cytoplasmic granules called glycolytic bodies (G bodies) in hypoxic stress in yeast, C. elegans, and mammalian cells (Jang et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017; Miura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies by the authors and others.

claim: In yeast, the presence of G bodies correlates with accelerated glucose consumption.
source: In yeast, the presence of G bodies correlates with accelerated glucose consumption, and impairing G body formation leads to the accumulation of upstream glycolytic metabolites (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: Impairing G body formation leads to the accumulation of upstream glycolytic metabolites.
source: In yeast, the presence of G bodies correlates with accelerated glucose consumption, and impairing G body formation leads to the accumulation of upstream glycolytic metabolites (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: During hypoxic stress, when oxidative phosphorylation is inhibited, G bodies form to enhance the rate of glycolysis by concentrating glycolysis enzymes.
source: These data suggest that during hypoxic stress, when oxidative phosphorylation is inhibited, G bodies form to enhance the rate of glycolysis by concentrating glycolysis enzymes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of cited data from previous studies.

claim: In C. elegans, hypoxia rapidly induces the formation of foci containing glycolysis enzymes near presynaptic release sites in neurons.
source: In C. elegans, hypoxia rapidly induces the formation of foci containing glycolysis enzymes near presynaptic release sites in neurons (Jang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: A phosphofructokinase mutant incapable of punctate localization disrupts synaptic vesicle clustering in neurons.

evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: Coalescence of glycolysis enzymes promotes synaptic function.
source: A phosphofructokinase mutant incapable of punctate localization disrupts synaptic vesicle clustering in neurons, suggesting that coalescence of glycolysis enzymes promotes synaptic function (Jang et al., 2016).

source: Nearly half of these mRBPs were non-canonical RBPs that do not contain conventional RNA binding domains.

claim: Pfk2, Eno1, Eno2, and Fba1 bind RNA.
source: To validate RNA binding by glycolysis enzymes, we end-labeled potential RNAs crosslinked to TAP-tagged Pfk2, Eno1, Eno2, and Fba1 (Figure 1C, left panels) with γ−32-P ATP. The autoradiographs displayed the same migration pattern in SDS-PAGE as the immunoblots of the corresponding TAP-tagged glycolysis enzymes (Figure 1C, right panels), suggesting that the glycolysis enzymes Pfk2, Eno1, Eno2, and Fba1 bind RNA.
evidence: PAR-CLIP autoradiography and western blot validation demonstrate RNA binding.

claim: Pfk2 has 439 direct mRNA substrates with 559 discrete binding sites.
source: Specifically, there were 439 direct mRNA substrates of Pfk2 with 559 discrete binding sites, 1,001 mRNA substrates with 1432 binding sites for Eno1, and 721 mRNA substrates with 1014 binding sites for Fba1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right panels).

claim: Eno1 has 1,001 mRNA substrates with 1432 binding sites.
source: Specifically, there were 439 direct mRNA substrates of Pfk2 with 559 discrete binding sites, 1,001 mRNA substrates with 1432 binding sites for Eno1, and 721 mRNA substrates with 1014 binding sites for Fba1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, right panels).

claim: Fba1 has 721 mRNA substrates with 1014 binding sites.

claim: 131 mRNAs bind all three glycolysis enzymes (Pfk2, Fba1, Eno1).

claim: G body RIP-seq reflects association of mRNA with G bodies.
source: The percent of mRNAs within a single pixel (0.13 µm) of a G body center correlated with enrichment in G body IPs, suggesting that G body RIP-seq reflects association of mRNA with G bodies (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFISH validation of G body RIP-seq.

claim: Maximally 2% of a particular mRNA is localized to G bodies.
source: However, this represented only a small fraction of the total pool of mRNA, with maximally 2% of a particular mRNA being localized to G bodies.
evidence: This is a result from smFISH analysis.

claim: G body mRNAs were most enriched near G body centers, becoming more randomly distributed as the distance from G bodies increased.
source: Normalizing the cumulative distribution of distances from G body centers for each mRNA to the OLE1 distribution revealed that G body mRNAs were most enriched near G body centers, becoming more randomly distributed as the distance from G bodies increased (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an analysis of smFISH distance measurements.

claim: There is often a cluster of mRNAs around the periphery of G bodies.
source: We also noticed that there was often a cluster of mRNAs around the periphery of G bodies (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from smFISH imaging.

claim: G bodies induced by hypoxia contain mRNAs that are initially bound by glycolysis enzymes in normoxia.
source: Taken together, these data suggest G bodies induced by hypoxia contain mRNAs that are initially bound by glycolysis enzymes in normoxia, but only concentrate a small fraction of any given mRNA to G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined PAR-CLIP-seq, G body RIP-seq, and smFISH results.

claim: G bodies only concentrate a small fraction of any given mRNA.
source: Taken together, these data suggest G bodies induced by hypoxia contain mRNAs that are initially bound by glycolysis enzymes in normoxia, but only concentrate a small fraction of any given mRNA to G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFISH and G body RIP-seq results.

claim: MqsR is an RNase that preferentially cleaves RNA at GCU sequences.
source: We targeted an RNAse to nascent G bodies by fusing Pfk2 to E. coli MqsR, an RNase that preferentially cleaves RNA at GCU sequences, followed by a C-terminal Flag tag (Kasari et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Weak expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag was detected even in the absence of CuSO4.
source: We detected weak expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag even in the absence of CuSO4, consistent with weak activation of the CUP1 promoter in hypoxic conditions (Becerra et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on western blot data and cited literature on CUP1 promoter behavior.

claim: Cells treated with CuSO4 showed a dose-dependent increase in Pfk2-MqsR-Flag levels.
source: Cells treated with CuSO4 showed a dose-dependent increase in Pfk2-MqsR-Flag levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, top panels).
evidence: This is based on western blot data.

claim: At low concentrations of CuSO4 (5, 10 µM) in hypoxia, the Pfk2-MqsR-Flag fusion protein was targeted to G bodies and colocalized with Pfk2-GFP.
source: At low concentrations of CuSO4 (5, 10 µM) in hypoxia, the Pfk2-MqsR-Flag fusion protein was targeted to G bodies and colocalized with Pfk2-GFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data.

claim: RNase A could be induced and targeted to G bodies as a Pfk2-RNase A fusion protein.
source: Using this same approach, another RNase, RNase A, could also be induced and targeted to G bodies as a Pfk2-RNase A fusion protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on western blot and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Targeting Pfk2-MqsR-Flag to G bodies caused a robust reduction in the fraction of hypoxic cells with G bodies in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Targeting Pfk2-MqsR-Flag to G bodies caused a robust reduction in the fraction of hypoxic cells with G bodies in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in cells expressing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag.

claim: G body formation in hypoxic cells carrying a control vector was unaffected by CuSO4 treatment at all concentrations tested.
source: In contrast, G body formation in hypoxic cells carrying a control vector was unaffected by CuSO4 treatment at all concentrations tested (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in control cells.

claim: Even without induction, hypoxic cells carrying the Pfk2-MqsR-Flag plasmid showed a 20% decrease in G body formation.
source: Even without induction, hypoxic cells carrying the Pfk2-MqsR-Flag plasmid showed a 20% decrease in G body formation, consistent with the weak expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag under these conditions.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation without CuSO4 induction.

claim: CuSO4-induced expression of Pfk2-RNase A similarly inhibited G body formation.
source: CuSO4-induced expression of Pfk2-RNase A similarly inhibited G body formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in cells expressing Pfk2-RNase A.

claim: MqsA is the antitoxin that inhibits MqsR RNase.
source: The MqsR RNase is inhibited by its antitoxin, MqsA (Kasari et al., 2010; Yamaguchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: At both 0 and 50 µM CuSO4, G body formation in hypoxic cells was unaffected by induction of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA.
source: At both 0 and 50 µM CuSO4, G body formation in hypoxic cells was now unaffected by induction of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA (Figure 4C), indicating that MqsA effectively inhibited the G body-targeted MqsR RNase from disrupting G body formation.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in cells expressing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA.

claim: MqsA effectively inhibited the G body-targeted MqsR RNase from disrupting G body formation.
source: At both 0 and 50 µM CuSO4, G body formation in hypoxic cells was now unaffected by induction of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA (Figure 4C), indicating that MqsA effectively inhibited the G body-targeted MqsR RNase from disrupting G body formation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA experiment.

claim: G bodies appeared larger and brighter in Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA-expressing cells than in cells expressing a vector control.
source: G bodies appeared larger and brighter in Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA-expressing cells than in cells expressing a vector control, possibly due to overexpression of Pfk2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: A Pfk2-RNase AH12A mutant with decreased RNase activity was less effective at reducing G body formation than Pfk2-RNase Awild-type.
source: Similarly, a Pfk2-RNase AH12A mutant with decreased RNase activity was less effective at reducing G body formation than Pfk2-RNase Awild-type, especially at 100 µM CuSO4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation with the RNase A mutant.

claim: Pfk2-RNase AH12A possesses residual RNase activity.
source: Pfk2-RNase AH12A possesses residual RNase activity (Thompson and Raines, 1994), which likely contributes to the modest loss of G body formation.
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Inhibition of G body formation by RNase A and MqsR is due to their ribonuclease activity.
source: Thus, inhibition of G body formation by RNase A and MqsR is due to their ribonuclease activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experiments with RNase mutants and antitoxin.

claim: MqsR-Flag expression had no effect on G body formation in hypoxic cells.
source: Unlike Pfk2-MqsR-Flag expression, MqsR-Flag expression had no effect on G body formation in hypoxic cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in cells expressing MqsR-Flag alone.

claim: CuSO4 induction of hypoxic cells expressing Pfk2-RNase A led to a decrease in G body formation of Eno2, Cdc19, and Fba1 in a CuSO4 concentration-dependent manner.
source: In each case, CuSO4 induction of hypoxic cells expressing Pfk2-RNase A, but not the vector control, led to a decrease in G body formation in a CuSO4 concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation for multiple G body markers.

claim: Directing a functional RNase to sites of G body formation leads to loss of G bodies.
source: Taken together, directing a functional RNase to sites of G body formation leads to loss of G bodies, indicating that RNA is required for G body formation in vivo (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of all the RNase targeting experiments.

claim: RNA is required for G body formation in vivo.
source: Taken together, directing a functional RNase to sites of G body formation leads to loss of G bodies, indicating that RNA is required for G body formation in vivo (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNase targeting experiments.

claim: Immediately following shift from hypoxic to normoxic conditions and concomitant CuSO4 addition, Pfk2-MqsR-Flag carrying cells showed a modest reduction in G body formation compared to controls.
source: Immediately following shift from hypoxic to normoxic conditions and concomitant CuSO4 addition (i.e., '0 hr post-hypoxia' in Figure 5A; Figure 5B), Pfk2-MqsR-Flag carrying cells showed a modest reduction in G body formation compared to controls (Figure 5A,B), likely due to leaky expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag in hypoxia.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation at 0 hr post-hypoxia.

claim: After prolonged induction of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag in normoxic conditions ('20 hr post-hypoxia'), strong expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag was observed at 100 µM CuSO4.
source: After prolonged induction of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag in normoxic conditions ('20 hr post-hypoxia' in Figure 5D; Figure 5E), we observed strong expression of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag at 100 µM CuSO4 and low-level expression even in cells without addition of CuSO4 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on western blot data.

claim: A substantial proportion of cells (41–50%) with Pfk2-MqsR-Flag showed multiple puncta per cell after 20 hr post-hypoxia induction.
source: In contrast, a substantial proportion of cells (41–50%) with Pfk2-MqsR-Flag showed multiple puncta per cell (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is based on quantification of cells with multiple puncta.

claim: Pre-formed G bodies fracture into multiple structures in the presence of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag.
source: These data suggest that pre-formed G bodies fracture into multiple structures in the presence of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multiple puncta phenotype after RNase induction post-hypoxia.

claim: Nascent G body formation was inhibited by RNases in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that 1) Nascent G body formation was inhibited by RNases in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4A);
evidence: This is a summary of the RNase targeting experiments during G body formation.

claim: Inhibition of de novo G body formation required both RNase activity and targeting to the site of G body formation.
source: 2) Inhibition of de novo G body formation required both RNase activity and targeting to the site of G body formation (Figure 4C–E);
evidence: This is a summary of the experiments with RNase mutants, antitoxin, and untargeted RNase.

claim: Once formed, targeting an RNase to G bodies led to cells with multiple foci, suggesting fragmentation but not dissolution of G bodies.
source: 3) Once formed, targeting an RNase to G bodies led to cells with multiple foci, suggesting fragmentation but not dissolution of G bodies (Figure 5D–F);
evidence: This is a summary of the post-hypoxia RNase induction experiments.

claim: Once formed in hypoxia, G bodies could persist for tens of hours in normoxia.
source: and 4) Once formed in hypoxia, G bodies could persist for tens of hours in normoxia (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is based on observation of G bodies 20 hr after shift to normoxia.

claim: Pfk2 has an IDR in its N-terminal domain.
source: Pfk2 has such an IDR in its N-terminal domain (Figure 6A, blue box).
evidence: This is based on IUPRED disorder prediction.

claim: Deletion of an N-terminal IDR spanning amino acids 140–165 of Pfk2-GFP (Pfk2∆140-165-GFP) increased the number of cells forming multiple foci and decreased overall G body formation.
source: Our previous study demonstrated that deletion of an N-terminal IDR spanning amino acids 140–165 of Pfk2-GFP (Pfk2∆140-165-GFP) increased the number of cells forming multiple foci and decreased overall G body formation (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The Pfk2 N-terminal domain is conserved in S. cerevisiae (28.7% identity) and other yeast species.
source: The Pfk2 N-terminal domain is conserved in S. cerevisiae (28.7% identity) and other yeast species.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: The crystal structure of S. cerevisiae heterooctameric phosphofructokinase lacks the N-terminal region for both Pfk1 and Pfk2, due to proteolytic cleavage in sample preparation.
source: The crystal structure of S. cerevisiae heterooctameric phosphofructokinase (with four copies each of Pfk1 and Pfk2) lacks this region for both Pfk1 and Pfk2, due to proteolytic cleavage in sample preparation (Banaszak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The crystal structure of phosphofructokinase from Komegataella pastoris shows that the Pfk2 N-terminal domain resembles a glyoxylase domain and interacts with Pfk1.
source: However, the crystal structure of phosphofructokinase from a related yeast species, Komegataella pastoris (Sträter et al., 2011), shows that the Pfk2 N-terminal domain resembles a glyoxylase domain and interacts with Pfk1.
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Regions outside of the Pfk2 N-terminus also interact with Pfk1 in both crystal structures to form a heterooctamer with four Pfk2 and four Pfk1 molecules.
source: Regions outside of the Pfk2 N-terminus also interact with Pfk1 in both crystal structures to form a heterooctamer with four Pfk2 and four Pfk1 molecules.
evidence: This is cited from published literature on crystal structures.

claim: Multiple interaction domains provide the potential for multivalent Pfk2 interactions.
source: These multiple interaction domains provide the potential for multivalent Pfk2 interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural information.

claim: Cells expressing Pfk2∆1-202-GFP had drastically reduced puncta compared with full-length Pfk2-GFP.
source: Compared with full-length Pfk2-GFP, cells expressing Pfk2∆1-202-GFP had drastically reduced puncta (Figure 6C), suggesting that the N-terminal domain is required for either G body formation or Pfk2 localization to G bodies.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation with the deletion mutant.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Pfk2 is required for either G body formation or Pfk2 localization to G bodies.
source: Compared with full-length Pfk2-GFP, cells expressing Pfk2∆1-202-GFP had drastically reduced puncta (Figure 6C), suggesting that the N-terminal domain is required for either G body formation or Pfk2 localization to G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Pfk2∆1-202-GFP phenotype.

claim: The localization defect was much stronger in Pfk2∆1-202-GFP cells than in Pfk2∆140-165-GFP cells.
source: Notably, the localization defect was much stronger in Pfk2∆1-202-GFP cells, suggesting that the structured portions of the N-terminal domain act in concert with the disordered residues to promote localization to G bodies.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two deletion mutants.

claim: The structured portions of the N-terminal domain act in concert with the disordered residues to promote localization to G bodies.
source: Notably, the localization defect was much stronger in Pfk2∆1-202-GFP cells, suggesting that the structured portions of the N-terminal domain act in concert with the disordered residues to promote localization to G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparison between deletion mutants.

claim: When PFK21-202-gfp was integrated and replaced full-length endogenous PFK2, Pfk21-202-GFP did not form puncta.
source: When PFK21-202-gfp was integrated and replaced full-length endogenous PFK2, Pfk21-202-GFP did not form puncta (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on imaging of the integrated Pfk21-202-GFP strain.

claim: When Pfk21-202-GFP was expressed from a plasmid in wild-type cells expressing endogenous full-length Pfk2, robust puncta formation was detected.
source: However, when Pfk21-202-GFP was expressed from a plasmid in wild-type cells expressing endogenous full-length Pfk2, we detected robust puncta formation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on imaging of cells with plasmid-expressed Pfk21-202-GFP.

claim: The N-terminal region of Pfk2 is not sufficient for G body localization, but requires interaction with full-length Pfk2 for recruitment to G bodies.
source: These data suggest that the N-terminal region of Pfk2 is not sufficient for G body localization, but requires interaction with full-length Pfk2 for recruitment to G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Pfk21-202-GFP experiments.

claim: The frequency of hypoxic cells with Pfk1-GFP puncta was reduced in pfk2∆ cells compared to wild-type.
source: The frequency of hypoxic cells with Pfk1-GFP puncta was reduced in pfk2∆ cells compared to wild-type, suggesting that Pfk1 is recruited to G bodies in concert with Pfk2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on quantification of Pfk1-GFP localization in wild-type and pfk2∆ cells.

claim: Pfk1 is recruited to G bodies in concert with Pfk2.
source: The frequency of hypoxic cells with Pfk1-GFP puncta was reduced in pfk2∆ cells compared to wild-type, suggesting that Pfk1 is recruited to G bodies in concert with Pfk2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Pfk1-GFP localization in pfk2∆ cells.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol specifically dissolves liquid-like structures purportedly due to its ability to disrupt weak hydrophobic interactions.
source: The alcohol 1,6-hexanediol specifically dissolves liquid-like structures purportedly due to its ability to disrupt weak hydrophobic interactions, and therefore has been used to discern liquid-like from solid-like granules (Kroschwald et al., 2017; Kroschwald et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: No significant loss of G bodies was observed after 1 hr treatment with 5% 1,6-hexanediol.
source: We noticed no significant loss of G bodies after 1 hr treatment, whereas untreated cells showed a modest loss of G bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation after 1,6-hexanediol treatment.

claim: The loss of G bodies in the control condition was likely due to continued cell division, which is inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol.
source: The loss of G bodies in the control condition was likely due to continued cell division, which is inhibited by 1,6-hexanediol (Kroschwald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited literature.

claim: G bodies in 1,6-hexanediol treated cells appeared smaller than those in untreated cells.
source: However, G bodies in 1,6-hexanediol treated cells appeared smaller than those in untreated cells.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: In 1,6-hexanediol treated cells, the average σX (0.72 +/– 0.055 µm) and σY (0.74 +/– 0.060 µm) values were lower than untreated cells (1.1 +/– 0.070 µm and 1.1 +/– 0.067 µm, respectively), indicating a smaller granule radius.
source: In 1,6-hexanediol treated cells, the average σX (0.72 +/– 0.055 µm) and σY (0.74 +/– 0.060 µm) values were lower than untreated cells (1.1 +/– 0.070 µm and 1.1 +/– 0.067 µm, respectively), indicating a smaller granule radius (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body size by Gaussian fitting.

claim: The amplitude was lower in the 1,6-hexanediol treated cells (12,054 +/– 857 A.U. compared to 18,519 +/– 1308 A.U.), indicating reduced total fluorescence in the granules.
source: Additionally, the amplitude was lower in the 1,6-hexanediol treated cells (12,054 +/– 857 A.U. compared to 18,519 +/– 1308 A.U.), indicating reduced total fluorescence in the granules.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body fluorescence by Gaussian fitting.

claim: While 1,6-hexanediol does not fully dissolve G bodies, it can reduce their size.
source: Thus, while 1,6-hexanediol does not fully dissolve G bodies, it can reduce their size.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the 1,6-hexanediol treatment results.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol treatment of glucose-starved cells disrupted P bodies labeled with Edc3-GFP.
source: As a control, we verified that 1,6-hexanediol treatment of glucose-starved cells disrupted P bodies labeled with Edc3-GFP, but caused only a small and not significant loss of stress granules labeled with Pab1-GFP (Kroschwald et al., 2015; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of P body and stress granule formation after 1,6-hexanediol treatment.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol treatment of glucose-starved cells caused only a small and not significant loss of stress granules labeled with Pab1-GFP.
source: As a control, we verified that 1,6-hexanediol treatment of glucose-starved cells disrupted P bodies labeled with Edc3-GFP, but caused only a small and not significant loss of stress granules labeled with Pab1-GFP (Kroschwald et al., 2015; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of stress granule formation after 1,6-hexanediol treatment.

claim: Addition of 1,6-hexanediol to the starvation media inhibited the formation of P bodies but not stress granules.
source: As a control, we verified that addition of 1,6-hexanediol to the starvation media inhibited the formation of P bodies but not stress granules (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C; Kroschwald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on quantification of P body and stress granule formation during starvation with 1,6-hexanediol.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol treatment of Pfk2-GFP wild-type cells during growth in hypoxia did not affect nascent G body formation.
source: We found that 1,6-hexanediol treatment of Pfk2-GFP wild-type cells during growth in hypoxia did not affect nascent G body formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), indicating that 1,6-hexanediol cannot prevent nucleation of G bodies.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation during hypoxia with 1,6-hexanediol.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol cannot prevent nucleation of G bodies.
source: We found that 1,6-hexanediol treatment of Pfk2-GFP wild-type cells during growth in hypoxia did not affect nascent G body formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), indicating that 1,6-hexanediol cannot prevent nucleation of G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 1,6-hexanediol treatment during hypoxia.

claim: Cells lacking Snf1 had decreased G body formation and frequently formed multiple smaller foci per cell.
source: We previously demonstrated that cells lacking Snf1, the yeast ortholog of AMP-activated protein kinase, had decreased G body formation and frequently formed multiple smaller foci per cell, rather than the single foci observed in wild type cells (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol treatment of snf1∆ cells increased the frequency of cells with a single Pfk2-GFP labeled G body.
source: Unexpectedly, 1,6-hexanediol treatment of snf1∆ cells increased the frequency of cells with a single Pfk2-GFP labeled G body (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), such that they appeared superficially wild type.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body formation in snf1∆ cells with 1,6-hexanediol.

claim: 1,6-hexanediol promotes Pfk2-GFP aggregation in snf1∆ cells subjected to hypoxia.
source: Therefore, 1,6-hexanediol promotes Pfk2-GFP aggregation in snf1∆ cells subjected to hypoxia, although this mode of aggregation may differ from normal G body formation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the snf1∆ 1,6-hexanediol treatment results.

claim: Similar results have been reported with extended treatments of high concentrations of 1,6-hexanediol for yeast P-bodies.
source: Similar results have been reported with extended treatments of high concentrations of 1,6-hexanediol for yeast P-bodies (Wheeler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: G bodies are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol and thus similar in physical properties to yeast stress granules.
source: Together, these findings suggest that G bodies are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol and thus similar in physical properties to yeast stress granules.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of all the 1,6-hexanediol experiments.

claim: There was very weak recovery (9.5% in YPD and 15% in SMD) of Pfk2-GFP after photobleaching.
source: Despite much of the fluorescence in the cell residing in G bodies, we were able to detect some recovery of Pfk2-GFP in yeast grown in YPD as well as in synthetic media (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A). However, there was very weak recovery (9.5% in YPD and 15% in SMD) and the half time of recovery was on the order of minutes.
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis of Pfk2-GFP.

claim: The half time of recovery of Pfk2-GFP was on the order of minutes.
source: Despite much of the fluorescence in the cell residing in G bodies, we were able to detect some recovery of Pfk2-GFP in yeast grown in YPD as well as in synthetic media (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A). However, there was very weak recovery (9.5% in YPD and 15% in SMD) and the half time of recovery was on the order of minutes.
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis of Pfk2-GFP.

claim: Fba1-GFP had substantially more recovery (28%) but with a similar half time of recovery (25 min).
source: Fba1-GFP had substantially more recovery (28%) but with a similar half time of recovery (25 min) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis of Fba1-GFP.

claim: Eno2-GFP displayed recovery, but with dynamics that appeared linear and did not fit to an exponential model.
source: Eno2-GFP also displayed recovery, but with dynamics that appeared linear and did not fit to an exponential model (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis of Eno2-GFP.

claim: Cells expressing Pfk2D348S-MqsR-Flag had slightly greater overall percentage of recovery (13% vs. 4.1%) compared to vector control.
source: Surprisingly, we detected slightly greater overall percentage of recovery (13% vs. 4.1%) for cells expressing Pfk2D348S-MqsR-Flag, although the weak recovery was more rapid (5.7 min vs. 10.6 min) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis with RNase treatment.

claim: When RNA is slightly depleted from G bodies by targeted RNase treatment, there is a modest enhancement in recovery of Pfk2-GFP.
source: Taken together, when RNA is slightly depleted from G bodies by targeted RNase treatment, there is a modest enhancement in recovery of Pfk2-GFP, indicating that Pfk2 is more stably associated with G bodies in the absence of RNase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP results with RNase treatment.

claim: Pfk2 is more stably associated with G bodies in the absence of RNase.
source: Taken together, when RNA is slightly depleted from G bodies by targeted RNase treatment, there is a modest enhancement in recovery of Pfk2-GFP, indicating that Pfk2 is more stably associated with G bodies in the absence of RNase.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP results with RNase treatment.

claim: RNA may promote stronger binding of Pfk2-GFP in G bodies.
source: Thus, RNA may promote stronger binding of Pfk2-GFP in G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP results with RNase treatment.

claim: Yeast cells display multiple Pfk2-GFP foci at early time points in hypoxia but only a single focus at later timepoints.
source: Consistent with fusion events in G body biogenesis, yeast cells display multiple Pfk2-GFP foci at early time points in hypoxia but only a single focus at later timepoints (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: G bodies moved throughout the cell during time-lapse imaging.
source: G bodies moved throughout the cell (Figure 7A,B; Figure 7—video 1, Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging of mating cells.

claim: When a G body from one mating cell type met a G body from the other mating cell type, they were able to fuse into a single G body in the mated diploid cell.
source: When a G body from one mating cell type met a G body from the other mating cell type, they were able to fuse into a single G body in the mated diploid cell.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging of mating cells.

claim: G body fusion occurred over longer timescales: from as short as 2 min to as long as 60 min, with a median of 18 min from initial contact to fusion.
source: However, unlike granules in liquid-like states, G body fusion occurred over longer timescales: from as short as 2 min to as long as 60 min, with a median of 18 min from initial contact to fusion to form a single G body (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on quantification of fusion times from time-lapse imaging.

claim: Some G bodies stayed oblong in shape when fused, while others became more spherical over tens of minutes.
source: Although some G bodies stayed oblong in shape when fused, others became more spherical over tens of minutes, suggesting that they behaved as gels with fusion over long timescales.
evidence: This is based on observation from time-lapse imaging.

claim: G bodies behave as gels with fusion over long timescales.
source: Although some G bodies stayed oblong in shape when fused, others became more spherical over tens of minutes, suggesting that they behaved as gels with fusion over long timescales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fusion dynamics.

claim: Some cells formed G bodies de novo during imaging, initially showing two distinct foci that became brighter and fused within 2 min of initial contact.
source: In accordance with these results, we also identified some cells that formed G bodies de novo during imaging. Initially, two distinct foci appeared from a diffuse cytoplasm, but over 60 min, these foci became brighter and fused within 2 min of initial contact (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: The fraction of mating cells with overlapping puncta increased over time from 3 hr to 24 hr.
source: We observed a high frequency of overlapping puncta, which increased over time. Overlapping puncta likely arose from fusion, although we cannot rule out that a subset arose from de novo granule formation in mating cells. The fraction of mating cells with adjacent and unassociated puncta decreased from 41% after 3 hr mating to only 11% after 24 hr mating, whereas the fraction with overlapping or fused puncta increased (Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body colocalization in mating cells over time.

claim: The fraction of mating cells with adjacent and unassociated puncta decreased from 41% after 3 hr mating to only 11% after 24 hr mating.
source: The fraction of mating cells with adjacent and unassociated puncta decreased from 41% after 3 hr mating to only 11% after 24 hr mating, whereas the fraction with overlapping or fused puncta increased (Figure 7D,E, Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body colocalization in mating cells over time.

claim: The progression from many particles to a single particle is consistent with fusion of granules.
source: The progression from many particles to a single particle is consistent with fusion of granules.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mating cell time course data.

claim: G bodies can fuse over minutes.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that G bodies can fuse over minutes and are largely insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol, properties reminiscent of gels.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the fusion and 1,6-hexanediol experiments.

claim: After 6 to 7 generations in hypoxia, vector control cells made up 65% of the culture when grown with Pfk2-MqsR-Flag expressing cells.
source: Strikingly, after 6 to 7 generations in hypoxia, we observed that vector control cells made up 65% of the culture when grown with Pfk2-MqsR-Flag expressing cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on the growth competition assay.

claim: The advantage in vector control cells was not due to extra Pfk2 catalytic activity.
source: The advantage in vector control cells was not due to extra Pfk2 catalytic activity as cells expressing Pfk2D348S-MqsR-Flag also had a disadvantage compared to vector control cells.
evidence: This is based on the growth competition assay with the Pfk2D348S mutant.

claim: Cells expressing MqsR alone also had a growth advantage over both Pfk2-MqsR-Flag and Pfk2D348S-MqsR-Flag expressing cells.
source: Furthermore, cells expressing MqsR alone also had a growth advantage over both Pfk2-MqsR-Flag and Pfk2D348S-MqsR-Flag expressing cells.
evidence: This is based on the growth competition assay.

claim: Cells expressing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA had only a small and not statistically significant increase in competitive fitness.
source: Cells expressing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag-MqsA had only a small and not statistically significant increase in competitive fitness (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on the growth competition assay.

claim: There is an increase in the population of cells with the vector control plasmid with increasing numbers of generations.
source: We observed an increase in the population of cells with the vector control plasmid with increasing numbers of generations (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C), consistent with a significant advantage for cells with G bodies.
evidence: This is based on the serial dilution growth competition assay.

claim: Cells with G bodies have a significant growth advantage.
source: We observed an increase in the population of cells with the vector control plasmid with increasing numbers of generations (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C), consistent with a significant advantage for cells with G bodies.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the growth competition assay results.

claim: Specifically depleting cells of G bodies by degrading RNA puts them at a competitive disadvantage to cells capable of forming G bodies.
source: Thus, specifically depleting cells of G bodies by degrading RNA puts them at a competitive disadvantage to cells capable of forming G bodies.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the growth competition assay.

claim: G bodies have properties of phase separated gels in vivo.
source: Here we report that G bodies have properties of phase separated gels in vivo.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings.

claim: Similar to yeast and mammalian stress granules, G bodies lack membranes and contain chaperones as well as proteins with intrinsically disordered regions.
source: First, similar to yeast and mammalian stress granules, G bodies lack membranes and contain chaperones as well as proteins with intrinsically disordered regions (Jain et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on data from this study and previous studies.

claim: G bodies were much less sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol than liquid phase-separated structures like P bodies.
source: Second, we found that G bodies were much less sensitive to 1,6-hexanediol than liquid phase-separated structures like P bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), extending their similarities to stress granules.
evidence: This is based on the 1,6-hexanediol treatment experiments.

claim: The size of G bodies appears reduced after 1,6-hexanediol treatment, indicating partial dissolution of the granules.
source: However, their size appears reduced after 1,6-hexanediol treatment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), indicating partial dissolution of the granules.
evidence: This is based on quantification of G body size after 1,6-hexanediol treatment.

claim: The slow fusion dynamics of G bodies are consistent with the weak, but measurable exchange with the cytoplasm observed by FRAP of whole G bodies.
source: The slow fusion dynamics of G bodies are consistent with the weak, but measurable exchange with the cytoplasm observed by FRAP of whole G bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting fusion dynamics with FRAP results.

claim: Formation of G bodies when cells are transitioned to hypoxia involves fusion of smaller granules into larger structures.
source: Indeed, formation of G bodies when cells are transitioned to hypoxia involves fusion of smaller granules into larger structures.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging observations.

claim: Early fusion events were insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol due to the presence of single foci even after extended 1,6-hexanediol treatment during hypoxia.
source: Early fusion events were insensitive to 1,6-hexanediol due to the presence of single foci even after extended 1,6-hexanediol treatment during hypoxia (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the 1,6-hexanediol treatment during hypoxia experiments.

claim: Even after extended periods in hypoxia, G bodies fuse in mating cells.
source: Additionally, even after extended periods in hypoxia, G bodies fuse in mating cells, demonstrating that 'mature' G bodies can still fuse (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse imaging of mating cells.

claim: Like stress granule cores, G bodies can be purified intact.
source: Like stress granule cores, which can be isolated and are stable in a lysate, G bodies can be purified intact (Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on data from a previous study.

claim: Stress granules can disperse on the order of tens of minutes following removal of stress.
source: However, unlike stress granules, which can disperse on the order of tens of minutes following removal of stress, and nucleoli, which rapidly assemble and disassemble during mitosis (Brangwynne et al., 2011; Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2008; Walters et al., 2015), G bodies can persist for tens of hours as revealed in our experiments inducing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag following hypoxic incubation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Nucleoli rapidly assemble and disassemble during mitosis.
source: However, unlike stress granules, which can disperse on the order of tens of minutes following removal of stress, and nucleoli, which rapidly assemble and disassemble during mitosis (Brangwynne et al., 2011; Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2008; Walters et al., 2015), G bodies can persist for tens of hours as revealed in our experiments inducing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag following hypoxic incubation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: G bodies can persist for tens of hours.
source: However, unlike stress granules, which can disperse on the order of tens of minutes following removal of stress, and nucleoli, which rapidly assemble and disassemble during mitosis (Brangwynne et al., 2011; Feric et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Tsai et al., 2008; Walters et al., 2015), G bodies can persist for tens of hours as revealed in our experiments inducing Pfk2-MqsR-Flag following hypoxic incubation (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the post-hypoxia RNase induction experiments.

claim: G bodies initially form from a liquid state and gradually solidify, becoming more similar to protein aggregates over time.
source: One possibility is that G bodies initially form from a liquid state and gradually solidify, becoming more similar to protein aggregates of FUS and IDRs of other proteins over time (Lin et al., 2015; Mateju et al., 2017; Murakami et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited literature.

claim: G bodies, once formed, can be disrupted by the targeting of an RNase, demonstrating that they are not static.
source: However, G bodies, once formed, can be disrupted by the targeting of an RNase, demonstrating that they are not static.
evidence: This is based on the post-hypoxia RNase targeting experiments.

claim: The effect of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag induced after hypoxic treatment was largely independent of the concentration of CuSO4 added.
source: The effect of Pfk2-MqsR-Flag induced after hypoxic treatment (when G bodies have already formed) was largely independent of the concentration of CuSO4 added (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on quantification of the post-hypoxia RNase induction experiments.

claim: A small amount of RNA degradation was sufficient for G body fragmentation.
source: Thus, a small amount of RNA degradation was sufficient for G body fragmentation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the post-hypoxia RNase induction results.

claim: The fragmented foci induced after hypoxic treatment appeared larger than single puncta in vector control cells.
source: The fragmented foci induced after hypoxic treatment appeared larger than single puncta in vector control cells (Figure 5), suggesting additional Pfk2-GFP could accumulate in these puncta in the absence of RNA.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: Additional Pfk2-GFP could accumulate in fragmented puncta in the absence of RNA.
source: The fragmented foci induced after hypoxic treatment appeared larger than single puncta in vector control cells (Figure 5), suggesting additional Pfk2-GFP could accumulate in these puncta in the absence of RNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation of larger fragmented foci.

claim: RNA is primarily required for G body fusion and nucleation.
source: This is consistent with RNA primarily being required for G body fusion and nucleation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNase targeting experiments.

claim: Both the N- and C-terminal domains of Pfk2 are necessary but not sufficient for G body recruitment.
source: Both the N- and C-terminal domains of Pfk2 are necessary but not sufficient for G body recruitment (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the Pfk2 deletion and truncation experiments.

claim: Pfk1 is recruited to G bodies via an interaction with Pfk2.
source: Pfk1 is recruited to G bodies via an interaction with Pfk2 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on the Pfk1-GFP localization in pfk2∆ cells.

claim: Protein-RNA interactions are required for G body formation.
source: Additionally, protein-RNA interactions are required for G body formation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the RNase targeting experiments.

claim: Multivalent interactions are necessary for phase separation and can drive granule formation.
source: Such multivalent interactions are necessary for phase separation and can drive granule formation (Hyman et al., 2014; Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: RNA is required for G body stability or integrity.
source: Degradation of RNA in existing G bodies led to multiple puncta, suggesting that RNA is required for G body stability or integrity (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the post-hypoxia RNase targeting experiments.

claim: FRAP data indicated that Pfk2-GFP in G bodies targeted by a weak induction of RNase was slightly more dynamic than untreated G bodies.
source: Furthermore, FRAP data indicated that Pfk2-GFP in G bodies targeted by a weak induction of RNase was slightly more dynamic than untreated G bodies, suggesting that RNA contributes to Pfk2 recruitment to G bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on FRAP analysis with RNase treatment.

claim: RNA contributes to Pfk2 recruitment to G bodies.
source: Furthermore, FRAP data indicated that Pfk2-GFP in G bodies targeted by a weak induction of RNase was slightly more dynamic than untreated G bodies, suggesting that RNA contributes to Pfk2 recruitment to G bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRAP results with RNase treatment.

claim: A comprehensive picture of an extensive glycolysis enzyme-bound transcriptome is emerging.
source: By PAR-CLIP-seq, a comprehensive picture of an extensive glycolysis enzyme-bound transcriptome is emerging (Figure 2; Shchepachev et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on PAR-CLIP-seq data from this study and cited literature.

claim: Glycolysis enzymes bind similar transcripts primarily in the 3' UTRs and coding regions of their substrate mRNAs.
source: Intriguingly, these enzymes bind similar transcripts primarily in the 3' UTRs and coding regions of their substrate mRNAs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on PAR-CLIP-seq binding site analysis.

claim: A common set of transcripts bound by multiple glycolysis enzymes in normoxic conditions was identified.
source: We identified a common set of transcripts bound by multiple glycolysis enzymes in normoxic conditions (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on PAR-CLIP-seq analysis.

claim: Many mRNA substrates of glycolysis enzymes were recruited along with their protein binding partners to G bodies in hypoxia.
source: We determined, by RIP-qPCR and RIP-seq of purified G bodies, that many of these mRNA substrates were then recruited along with their protein binding partners to G bodies in hypoxia (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on G body RIP-qPCR and RIP-seq data.

claim: smFISH of G body-associated RNAs revealed the extent to which RNA colocalization with G bodies correlated with the degree of enrichment.
source: smFISH of G body-associated RNAs revealed the extent to which RNA colocalization with G bodies correlated with the degree of enrichment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on smFISH analysis.

claim: No RNA analyzed by smFISH was strongly enriched in G bodies.
source: Surprisingly, no RNA analyzed by smFISH was strongly enriched in G bodies, although some RNAs partitioned up to 2-fold more in G bodies than others.
evidence: This is based on smFISH analysis.

claim: While RNAs are required for G body formation, there may be only modest preference for which specific RNA species are recruited to G bodies, as long as they bind glycolysis enzymes.
source: Therefore, while RNAs are required for G body formation, there may be only modest preference for which specific RNA species are recruited to G bodies, as long as they bind glycolysis enzymes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFISH and G body RIP-seq results.

claim: RNA serves as a scaffold for G body nucleation and growth.
source: We propose a model in which RNA serves as a scaffold for G body nucleation and growth.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: Addition of RNA promotes the aggregation of the glycolysis enzyme, Cdc19, in vitro.
source: Consistent with this model, addition of RNA promotes the aggregation of the glycolysis enzyme, Cdc19, in vitro (Saad et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Among the commonly bound transcripts were a number of mRNAs encoding the glycolysis enzymes themselves.
source: Among the commonly bound transcripts were a number of mRNAs encoding the glycolysis enzymes themselves.
evidence: This is based on PAR-CLIP-seq analysis.

claim: Weak, dynamic interactions between G body components with RNA and with each other would allow for the growth of G bodies.
source: Weak, dynamic interactions between G body components with RNA and with each other would allow for the growth of G bodies.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data.

claim: RNA interactions with glycolysis enzymes can facilitate post-transcriptional regulation of the pathway.
source: It has been proposed that RNA interactions with glycolysis enzymes can facilitate post-transcriptional regulation of the pathway (Matia-González et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Concentration of nascent proteins due to spatially segregated translation of glycolysis enzyme mRNAs could contribute to G body formation.
source: This mode of regulation could additionally contribute to G body formation through concentration of nascent proteins due to spatially segregated translation of glycolysis enzyme mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Interactions with glycolysis enzyme mRNAs may specifically facilitate multivalent interactions of glycolysis enzymes with RNA by providing a common set of substrates.
source: Interactions with glycolysis enzyme mRNAs may specifically facilitate multivalent interactions of glycolysis enzymes with RNA by providing a common set of substrates.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism.

claim: Hypoxia may weaken interactions of glycolysis enzymes with RNAs, allowing for G bodies to form via protein-protein interactions.
source: Alternatively, hypoxia may weaken interactions of glycolysis enzymes with RNAs, allowing for G bodies to form via protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: RNAs localized peripherally to G bodies may allow G bodies to fuse by binding the glycolysis enzymes in other G bodies.
source: Many RNAs are localized peripherally to G bodies (Figure 3). These RNAs may then allow G bodies to fuse by binding the glycolysis enzymes in other G bodies, explaining the loss of foci with loss of RNA.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of peripheral RNAs.

claim: Phase separation is emerging as a new mechanism to achieve spatial organization of metabolic pathways.
source: Although spatial organization of pathways to concentrate constituent enzymes is not novel, phase separation is emerging as a new mechanism to achieve this type of organization.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field.

claim: Glycolysis enzymes are concentrated in membrane-bound compartments called glycosomes in various protozoa, including in Trypanosoma brucei.
source: Even for glycolysis, pathway compartmentalization is known to occur; glycolysis enzymes are concentrated in membrane-bound compartments called glycosomes in various protozoa, including in Trypanosoma brucei, which can survive in anaerobic conditions (Michels et al., 2006; Opperdoes, 1987).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Phase separation is mechanistically distinct from membrane-bound compartmentalization in that it does not require formation of a membrane or specific transporters.
source: However, phase separation is mechanistically distinct in that it does not require formation of a membrane or specific transporters.
evidence: This is a comparison of mechanisms.

claim: Three recent studies have demonstrated glycolysis enzyme coalescence in hypoxia, which is associated with increased rates of glucose flux.
source: Three recent studies have demonstrated glycolysis enzyme coalescence in hypoxia, which is associated with increased rates of glucose flux (Jang et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017; Miura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: G bodies and glycosomes may represent a case of convergent evolution.
source: Thus, G bodies and glycosomes may represent a case of convergent evolution.
evidence: This is speculation based on the comparison of G bodies and glycosomes.

claim: Cancer cell lines form small aggregates of glycolysis enzymes even in the presence of oxygen.
source: Furthermore, cancer cell lines form small aggregates of glycolysis enzymes even in the presence of oxygen, suggesting that concentrating glycolysis enzymes is a highly conserved process (Kohnhorst et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Concentrating glycolysis enzymes is a highly conserved process.
source: Furthermore, cancer cell lines form small aggregates of glycolysis enzymes even in the presence of oxygen, suggesting that concentrating glycolysis enzymes is a highly conserved process (Kohnhorst et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of cited data.

claim: Pyrenoids enhance the rate of carbon fixation in Chlamydomonas by concentrating CO2 in the presence of ribulose 1,5 bisphosphate carboxylase oxygenase (RuBisCo).
source: Additionally, pyrenoids, which enhance the rate of carbon fixation in Chlamydomonas by concentrating CO2 in the presence of ribulose 1,5 bisphosphate carboxylase oxygenase (RuBisCo), were shown to form via phase separation (Freeman Rosenzweig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Pyrenoids form via phase separation.
source: Additionally, pyrenoids, which enhance the rate of carbon fixation in Chlamydomonas by concentrating CO2 in the presence of ribulose 1,5 bisphosphate carboxylase oxygenase (RuBisCo), were shown to form via phase separation (Freeman Rosenzweig et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Carbon metabolism can be controlled both at the level of fixation and harvesting via phase separation into distinct compartments.
source: Carbon metabolism, then, can be controlled both at the level of fixation and harvesting via phase separation into distinct compartments.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the examples of pyrenoids and G bodies.

claim: Cells capable of forming G bodies possess a distinct growth advantage over multiple generations when co-cultured with cells that cannot form G bodies.
source: Here, we demonstrate that cells capable of forming G bodies possess a distinct growth advantage over multiple generations when co-cultured with cells that cannot form G bodies (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the growth competition assay.

claim: RNA induced coalescence of glycolysis enzymes promotes proliferation in hypoxia, likely by enhancing rates of glycolysis.
source: Thus, RNA induced coalescence of glycolysis enzymes promotes proliferation in hypoxia, likely by enhancing rates of glycolysis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the growth competition assay results.

claim: Phase separation can enhance reaction rates through decreased substrate inhibition.
source: Recent in vitro measurements of dextranase activity in artificial liquid-liquid phase separated compartments suggest that phase separation can enhance reaction rates through decreased substrate inhibition (Kojima and Takayama, 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Phosphofructokinase mediates one of the irreversible steps in glycolysis.
source: The G body resident factor phosphofructokinase mediates one of the irreversible steps in glycolysis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Phosphofructokinase is subject to substrate inhibition by ATP.
source: It is also subject to substrate inhibition by ATP and may experience increased specific activity akin to release from substrate inhibition when dextranase undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Phosphofructokinase may experience increased specific activity akin to release from substrate inhibition when in phase separated compartments.
source: It is also subject to substrate inhibition by ATP and may experience increased specific activity akin to release from substrate inhibition when dextranase undergoes liquid-liquid phase separation.
evidence: This is speculation based on cited literature about dextranase.

claim: Purinosomes are thought to enhance pathway activity through substrate channeling.
source: However, purinosomes, which are complexes composed of purine biosynthesis enzymes, are thought to enhance pathway activity through substrate channeling (An et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Concentrating enzymes in RNP granules may enhance reaction flux rates via concentrating intermediate metabolites.
source: Concentrating enzymes in RNP granules may achieve similar results or enhance reaction flux rates via concentrating intermediate metabolites.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: Concentration of energy producing enzymes with their cognate mRNAs may facilitate enhanced translation of the glycolysis enzymes, thus promoting pathway activity without increasing specific activity of the enzymes.
source: Alternatively, concentration of energy producing enzymes with their cognate mRNAs may facilitate enhanced translation of the glycolysis enzymes, thus promoting pathway activity without increasing specific activity of the enzymes.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.
